clauses.reason: The approving paragraph of Executive Order 6658 reads: "Now, Therefore, I, Franklin D. Roosevelt, President of the United States, pursuant to the authority vested in me by Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act, approved June 16, 1933, and otherwise, do adopt and approve the report, recommendations and findings of the Administrator and do order that the said Code of Fair Competition be and it is hereby approved," and continues with a stay condition (its own clause). The approval states no period, until-date or provisional approval; the 1944 WPA list describes it as "conditionally approved", which refers to the stay. The approval was code-dependent: under section 3(b) of the Act the approved provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade or industry, under section 3(c) the district courts could restrain violations, and under section 3(f) a violation was a misdemeanor, so the approval operated only through section 3. Section 2 of S.J. Res. 113, approved June 14, 1935, provides "All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed". The resolution states no effective date other than its approval, so the approval ceased to operate on June 14, 1935. No held record shows this code cancelled or suspended before June 14, 1935. June 16, 1935 is not an end date: section 1 of the same resolution replaced the original two-year expiry of Title I with April 1, 1936, and nothing in the resolution defers section 2. Schechter (May 27, 1935) is recorded as a validity characterization, not as an end date.

The stay condition of Executive Order 6658 reads: "subject to the following condition: that the provisions of Article VI, Section 6, subsection (i), be stayed until the Administrator, after further study and a public hearing, shall order otherwise.". It stays one provision of the code, Article VI, Section 6, subsection (i), until the Administrator, after further study and a public hearing, orders otherwise. The stated end is a contingent event (the Administrator's later order) with no date. No held text records such an order, and the held order texts do not include the Administrator's orders; the stay is therefore recorded as ending no later than the repeal, and it is not recorded as having ended earlier. The stay modifies only a provision of the approved code and has no operation apart from it, so it fell with the approval when section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 repealed the provisions delegating power to approve codes and providing for their enforcement, effective on its approval, June 14, 1935. If a Presidential or Administrator order lifting the stay is later held for a date before June 14, 1935, it becomes the first end of this clause. June 16, 1935 is not an end date: section 1 of the same resolution replaced the original two-year expiry of Title I with April 1, 1936, and nothing in the resolution defers section 2.

inventory_overrides.reason: The machine inventory has one clause for the whole paragraph. The paragraph contains two commands, the approval and the stay of Article VI, Section 6, subsection (i), which has a contingent end of its own; they are separated so that each gets its own end reasoning.
Second command of the same order: the stay of Article VI, Section 6, subsection (i), until the Administrator orders otherwise.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 6658 (March 27, 1934) approves the Code of Fair Competition for the Shoe Rebuilding Trade under Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act. The held text is the American Presidency Project transcription (grade mirror_transcription, acceptable_as_original false; Common Crawl capture 2025-10-15T16:13:18Z); the standing note applies: original not yet held; replace and re-check quotes when an official copy is retrieved. The order has two commands: the approval, and the stay of Article VI, Section 6, subsection (i), until the Administrator orders otherwise. Because each command is dependent on the code and no held record shows an earlier end, the first end is the statutory repeal of the code approval and enforcement provisions by section 2 of S.J. Res. 113, effective June 14, 1935. Schechter, decided May 27, 1935, held the section 3 delegation unconstitutional; that is recorded as a validity characterization (void from issuance under then-prevailing doctrine), not as an end date, because the judgment cancelled no approval. The antitrust-exemption proviso of the resolution is not settled by the held text for past action; whatever survives is an accrued effect, not continued operation of the approval.

savings.reason: Acts done and liabilities incurred under the approved code before June 14, 1935 are accrued effects of the repealed approval, and the section 5 antitrust exemption for completed action taken while the approval was in effect is likewise an accrued effect; it is preserved only for past action, and nothing in S.J. Res. 113 or in any held source continues the approval or its enforcement after June 14, 1935. No held source shows a prosecution or injunction continued under this approval after that date.

United States, 295 U.S. 495, held the Live Poultry Code provisions in question invalid and reversed the conviction; recorded as the validity characterization of every section 3 approval, not as an end of this approval, because the judgment did not cancel or withdraw this order.

source_notes.reason: The opinion of the Court states: "We think that the code-making authority thus conferred is an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power." The holding reaches section 3 approvals generally and is recorded as validity context only.
